fullGuide.summary: Communication access for people who are Deaf or hard of hearing is both a legal requirement and basic respect. A few practices make a real difference, and understanding a little about Deaf culture goes a long way. A note on culture and language. Many Deaf people, with a capital D, see themselves as part of a cultural and linguistic community whose language is American Sign Language, not as people with a medical loss. They often prefer identity-first language, Deaf person. Others, often those who are hard of hearing or who lost hearing later, may identify differently. Follow each person's own preference. Key practices. • Provide qualified interpreters for anything important, at no cost, and arrange them early. American Sign Language is its own language, not signed English, and a qualified interpreter matters. • Do not rely on a family member or a child to interpret. • When using an interpreter, look at and speak to the Deaf person, not the interpreter. Use you, not he or she. • Offer real choices. Some people prefer interpreters, some video relay, some captioning, some writing back and forth. Ask what works for them. • Face the person, keep your face visible, and speak naturally.

fullGuide.summary: Employment First is Minnesota's policy that competitive, integrated employment is the first and expected option for working-age people with disabilities. The starting belief is simple and important: people with disabilities can work, want to work, and can earn a competitive wage in a regular workplace alongside coworkers without disabilities. The policy. The Olmstead Subcabinet adopted Minnesota's Employment First Policy in 2014, and in 2020 the Legislature wrote Employment First into state law. It directs state agencies to make employment the first option considered — meaning a person should be offered the chance to work and earn a competitive wage before being offered other day services or supports. What competitive integrated employment means. A real job, in the community, at a fair wage that is at least minimum wage, working alongside people without disabilities, with the same chances to advance. Not segregated, not sub-minimum, not a placeholder. How Minnesota supports it.

fullGuide.summary: The National CLAS Standards are 15 standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health. They help health and human services reduce disparities by making sure services respond to each person's culture, language, and communication needs. fullGuide.summary: Intersectionality is the idea that people hold more than one identity at once, and those identities combine to shape their experience in ways you cannot see by looking at any one of them alone. A Black woman with a disability does not experience race, then gender, then disability separately. She experiences all of them together, and the combination can create barriers that none of them would predict on its own. Why it matters in our work. If we only ever look at one category at a time, we miss people who fall between them. A program that works for white disabled people and for non-disabled people of color can still fail disabled people of color, and our data may never show it if we never look at the overlap. What it looks like in practice. • Look at the overlap, not just the column. When you break down data, look at combinations, not only single categories, while protecting small numbers. • Do not ask people to split themselves. A person should not have to choose which part of who they are matters today. • Notice who falls through the cracks. The people served worst are often those at the intersection of more than one underserved group. • Design for the margins.

fullGuide.summary: It is easy to measure how busy we are. It is harder, and far more important, to measure whether anything changed. Equity work fails quietly when we count activities and call it progress. The discipline is to separate activity from impact. Activity is what we did. Impact is what changed. • Activity: staff trained, policies reviewed, meetings held, requests answered. • Impact: disparities reduced, access improved, people who felt excluded now feel included, outcomes that no longer track with race or disability. Both matter, but do not confuse them. Training a hundred people is an activity. Whether those people now make fairer decisions is the impact. A program can be very busy and change nothing. How to measure honestly. • Break results down by group, because an average can hide the gap that is the whole point. • Set a baseline first. You cannot show change without knowing where you started. • Give every measure an owner, a threshold, and an action. A number nobody acts on is just decoration. • Watch for measures that flatter you. If a metric only ever shows success, it is probably measuring the wrong thing. The honest question.

fullGuide.summary: Change management is how you help people through a change so it actually sticks. A good idea can fail simply because the people affected were not brought along. Equity work is full of change, so this is a core skill. Why change is hard. People do not resist change so much as they resist loss, uncertainty, and feeling done to instead of done with. Most resistance is information: it tells you something about what people fear or do not yet understand. What helps change take hold. • Make the case. Explain why the change matters and what happens if nothing changes, in plain language. • Involve people early. People support what they help shape. Bring affected staff and communities in before the plan is final. • Be honest about the trade-offs. Name what is hard or uncertain. Trust grows when you do not oversell. • Support the transition. Give people training, time, and a place to ask questions and make mistakes. • Close the loop. Show what you heard and what you changed because of it. Silence reads as not listening. • Expect a dip. Things often feel worse before they feel better. Plan for it so it does not derail the work. Lead with respect. Change done to people breeds resistance.

It covers state and local government — every program, service, and activity a public entity provides. For the Disability Services Division it is not an outside rule to satisfy; it is the floor under everything we do. What Title Two requires, in plain terms: • Equal opportunity. fullGuide.summary: The situation A committed leader has been holding her team together through a long, demanding stretch, absorbing everyone's stress, being the steady one, never letting them see her strain, and never saying no. Lately she is exhausted, short, and flat about work she used to love, and she keeps pushing, because people are counting on her and she does not want to let them down. What is really going on This is the leader's particular load, the responsibility, the loneliness, the pressure to be steady for everyone, the emotional labor of holding others, carried without tending, heading toward burnout. It is not weakness or a failure of dedication; it is the predictable result of pouring out for a long time without refilling, and the very conscientiousness that makes her valuable is part of what is depleting her. How to think about it Sustaining herself is a condition of leading well, not self-indulgence, and a depleted leader cannot give what the team needs. Her steadiness is contagious, and so, eventually, is her depletion. Tending herself is also modeling: if she never sets boundaries or admits limits, she teaches her team that they cannot either.

fullGuide.summary: Autism is a natural variation in how people experience the world, think, communicate, and process senses. The neurodiversity view holds that autistic ways of being are differences to understand and support, not defects to fix. Our job is to support autistic people to live the lives they choose, on their own terms. A note on language. Many autistic people prefer identity-first language, autistic person, rather than person with autism, because they see autism as part of who they are. People First language is our default, but the respectful move is to follow each person's own preference. When you can, ask. What helps in practice. • Presume competence. Communication differences are not the same as an inability to understand or decide. Speak to the person as a capable adult. • Honor communication. Some autistic people speak, some use devices, some communicate in other ways. All of it is valid. Give time, and do not rush or finish sentences. • Respect sensory needs. Bright lights, loud rooms, and strong smells can be genuinely painful. Offer quieter options and let people regulate without judgment. • Be clear and predictable.

fullGuide.summary: Minnesota is home to eleven federally recognized Tribal Nations, each a sovereign government with the right to self-govern and self-determine. Our relationship with them is government-to-government, nation to state, not agency to stakeholder. That distinction shapes everything about how this work is done. What sovereignty means here. Tribal Nations are not one more community group to consult. They are governments. Minnesota law affirms their sovereignty and requires the state to build relationships on respect, understanding, and meaningful consultation. Each Tribe is distinct, with its own government, culture, and priorities. What meaningful consultation requires. • Government-to-government. The state engages Tribal Nations as full partners and equals. • Early and ongoing. Consultation begins at the earliest stages of a decision and continues throughout, not as a sign-off at the end. • Relationship-based. It depends on trust built over time, through people, not paperwork. • Respectful of difference. What works with one Tribal Nation may not fit another. How it works in our administration.

fullGuide.summary: This all-staff pathway turns equity inward, toward how we treat each other. It moves from what a healthy workplace culture looks like, through staff engagement and belonging, breaking silos and collaborating across units, inclusive communication, and cultural sensitivity among colleagues, into psychological safety and a culture of safety, and closes with managing workplace stress, conflict, and repair.
